opus-5.5.text:
I think for me it usually starts from a real pain point rather than from a paper idea. A lot of the projects I ended up working on, like XGBoost or TVM, came from moments where I was trying to get something done myself and found that the tools just weren't there, or they were too slow, or they only worked on one kind of hardware. When you feel that friction personally, it's a pretty good signal that other people are feeling it too.

The second thing I look at is whether the problem sits at an interface between layers. Machine learning systems is interesting because the field moves so fast at the top, with new models and new workloads, while the hardware underneath is also changing quickly. The gap between those two is where many of the most impactful problems live. So I ask: is there a mismatch between what the models need and what the system stack can deliver? If the answer is yes, and it's likely to persist for a while, that's worth investing in.

Third, I care about whether the work can become something people actually use. I like research that ends up as open source, because it forces you to be honest. If people pick it up, run it on their own problems, and it holds up, that's real validation. It also creates a feedback loop: the community tells you what's broken and what the next problem is, which often leads you to the next research question.

And finally, I try to think a bit ahead. You don't want to just optimize what's popular today. You want to ask what the world will look like in a few years. For example, thinking about how to bring large models to every device, not just big data centers, so more people can run and customize them. If you pick problems that align with where things are heading, and that you're genuinely excited to spend years on, the work tends to compound.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. That's a question I think about a lot, because there are so many directions you could go in ML systems, and the field moves fast enough that chasing every new thing is a recipe for never finishing anything.

The way I usually approach it is to look for a gap between what people want to do and what the current tools actually let them do. When I was working on XGBoost, that came out of a very practical frustration: I wanted a gradient boosting implementation that was fast, scaled, and handled the messy details like sparse data, and nothing I could find did all of that. The problem picked itself, in a sense, because I was my own first user.

With TVM, the motivation was a bit different but still grounded in a real tension. We had this explosion of models on one side, and this explosion of hardware on the other, from GPUs to phones to custom accelerators. Every combination required hand-tuned kernels, and that clearly wasn't going to scale. So the question became: can we build a compiler abstraction that lets us automate that? That's the kind of problem I like, where there's a structural mismatch that will only get worse over time, so solving it has a compounding payoff.

A few things I try to check before committing. First, is there a real pain point I can articulate concretely, ideally one I've felt myself? Second, is it a problem where a good abstraction or system design actually changes the game, rather than just a point optimization? And third, can we build something that people outside the lab will actually use? I care a lot about open source for this reason. Releasing the system and watching how people use it, and where they struggle, feeds back into the research and tells you what the next problem is.

I'd also say that I'm willing to stay on a direction for a long time. Machine learning compilation is something I've been pushing on for years now, through TVM and more recently with MLC-LLM, bringing large models onto all kinds of devices. The problem keeps evolving as models and hardware change, so you don't run out of interesting questions. Picking a direction with that kind of longevity is, I think, more valuable than picking the hottest topic of the month.

And honestly, part of it is taste and curiosity. Sometimes a problem just feels like it has depth, where the first solution raises three more questions. Those are usually the ones worth working on.

astra-6.text:
I usually start with a concrete bottleneck. If you’re trying to build or deploy a machine learning application, what is stopping you? Is it performance, memory, or the amount of engineering effort needed to make it work?

Then I ask whether that bottleneck points to a more general problem. You can spend a lot of time optimizing one particular workload, but I’m especially interested when solving that problem gives us an abstraction or a tool that helps with many workloads.

There’s also an iterative part to choosing problems. You build something, let people use it, and learn where your assumptions were wrong. That feedback often leads to the next research question. So for me, it’s a combination of a practical need, an opportunity for a general solution, and a way to test the idea in a real system.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, it usually starts with trying to build something and understanding what gets in the way. You might want to run a model on a new device, or make an experiment easier to reproduce, and discover that the existing tools don’t quite support it. That friction can be a starting point for research.

Then I ask whether the problem is specific to this application or whether there’s a more general question underneath it. Can we find an abstraction that helps with a whole class of workloads? And can we build a system to test whether that abstraction actually works?

I also like the feedback loop between research and users. When people use a system, they expose assumptions you didn’t realize you were making. So choosing the problem isn’t just one decision at the beginning. You build something, learn from how it’s used, and refine the question.
